name: Ceramide NP

card.summary: A skin-identical barrier lipid (also called Ceramide 3) in moisturizers that helps hold water in the skin, so it looks smoother, calmer and less dry.

quick.overview:
Ceramide NP, also labeled Ceramide 3, is a lipid of the same family as those that make up the skin's outer barrier. Ceramides, cholesterol and fatty acids form the matrix between surface skin cells that limits water loss.

In moisturizers it is used to support that barrier, which helps dry, flaky or sensitive skin look smoother and less red. Trials of ceramide-containing creams have studied dryness, rosacea redness and eczema flares.
quick.how: It is an ingredient in over-the-counter moisturizers, cleansers and serums, often alongside cholesterol, fatty acids, glycerin, panthenol or Centella asiatica. Products are typically applied once or twice daily, and hydration changes are usually measured over weeks.
quick.risks: A 2015 safety review calculated margins of safety for ceramide 3 in cosmetics and reported no safety concerns for products with less than 1% ceramide 3.[1] Skin products can still occasionally irritate.

lead: Ceramide NP, known on labels as Ceramide 3, is a ceramide of the phytoceramide NP class used in skincare.[1][2] Ceramides are a major component of the stratum corneum, the skin's outer layer, where together with cholesterol and free fatty acids they form a water-limiting barrier; the lipid matrix is roughly half ceramides by weight.[2]

People use it in moisturizers to support the barrier, so skin looks less dry and feels more comfortable. Ceramide levels in skin can fall with dry or polluted air, harsh sulfates, heat, UV exposure and aging.[2] Barrier lipids have been studied in atopic dermatitis, where lower ceramide levels have been reported.[3]
Several randomized trials have tested products containing Ceramide NP, usually combined with other ingredients, in dry, sensitive, rosacea-prone and eczema-prone skin.[4][5][6]

chain: Skin looks smoother, hydrated and calmer
angle.text: Ceramide NP is used to support the skin barrier so dry or sensitive skin looks and feels better. Users often layer it into a daily moisturizer.

paras: The skin barrier lipid matrix is about 50 percent ceramides, 25 percent cholesterol and 15 percent free fatty acids by weight.[2] A clinical review of skin lipids notes that human studies have suggested ceramide 1 and to some extent ceramide 3 may play a role in atopic dermatitis.[3] NP ceramides were reported lower in psoriatic scale.[2]

A 2015 risk assessment estimated margins of safety for ceramide 3 at 0.5 to 10 percent in different product types, finding lipsticks up to 10 percent and shampoos at 0.5 percent acceptable, face cream up to 3 percent, and no concerns for products with less than 1 percent ceramide 3.[1]

A randomized trial of a pseudo-ceramide spray in people with dry, sensitive skin found the stratum corneum NP/NS ceramide ratio rose with application over four weeks, while a control spray produced no change.[4] In 75 patients with erythematotelangiectatic rosacea taking oral minocycline, a moisturizer containing Centella asiatica, ceramide NP and panthenol was associated with rapid improvements in redness, hydration and quality of life by day 28.[5] A 12-week trial of an emollient containing ceramide 3, omega-6 fatty acids, licochalcone A and glycerol tested flare prevention in atopic dermatitis after steroid treatment.[6] These products contain several actives, so effects cannot be assigned to ceramide NP alone.
